section: Opposition precision and inferior king-and-pawn defense

positions.title: A c-pawn push changes the opposition — Pa2
positions.sourceLabel: P102 · Technical opposition and move order
positions.prompt: King opposition changes when the attacker goes via e4 or c4. The c3 pawn remains a reserve tempo but the defender can contest c4 and d5. White keeps a2 as an outside reserve tempo. Work both king routes and identify when an apparent pawn win gives the defender a tempo.
positions.replyReason: ...Kd6 and ...Kd5 actively oppose the escorting king; after c4 the newly advanced pawn may be attacked by the black king. In this variation, White keeps a2 as an outside reserve tempo.
positions.continuationReason: At the fifth ply White has increased pawn space, but Black is close enough to contest c4. The recorded five plies do not prove a forced promotion.
positions.explanation: A c-pawn push changes the opposition. Five-ply line d4e4 e6d6 e4f5 d6d5 c3c4. Resistance d4c4 e6d6 c4b5 d6d5 c3c4. Plausible different choice c3c4 e6d6 d4e4. King opposition changes when the attacker goes via e4 or c4. The c3 pawn remains a reserve tempo but the defender can contest c4 and d5. ...Kd6 and ...Kd5 actively oppose the escorting king; after c4 the newly advanced pawn may be attacked by the black king. Endpoint: White has increased pawn space, but Black is close enough to contest c4. The recorded five plies do not prove a forced promotion. Misconception: A fourth-rank passer is not automatically protected when the opposing king controls its new square. Pawn reserve: White keeps a2 as an outside reserve tempo. A concrete two-king draw after liquidation is exact only in the pure case; other WDL values require independent proof.

positions.title: Mirror-file defender: preserving a g-pawn against h3
positions.sourceLabel: P102 · Defending the worse pawn ending
positions.prompt: Black's advanced h3 pawn threatens the white g2 pawn, but the white king can reach g1 and answer ...h2+ by capturing the dangerous pawn. Calculate ...Kf5 and White's next king square before calling it a win; this is the reflected version of a typical last-pawn defense.
positions.replyReason: ...h2+ checks the king on g1. Kxh2 is legal because Black's king on g4 is too distant to defend h2. ...Kf5 then challenges White's g-pawn conversion.
positions.continuationReason: White retains g2 and has K g3, while Black has only its king after the h-pawn is removed. Conversion still requires accurate king play.
positions.explanation: Mirror-file original pawn-defense study. Main: h1g1 h3h2 g1h2 g4f5 h2g3. Alternative: h1g1 h3h2 g1h1 g4f5 h1h2; both involve the white king taking h2 on different tempi. Tempting pawn plan: h1g1 g4f5 g2g4, allowing the black king to attack the pawn from f5. Compare the black pawn h3's attack on g2 with its checking advance h2+. This differs from the a/b-file illustration and represents a distinct legal endgame position. No tablebase-perfect result is claimed beyond the removal of the black pawn in the demonstrated line.

defensiveStudy.defenderIdea: ...h2+ checks the king on g1. Kxh2 is legal because Black's king on g4 is too distant to defend h2. ...Kf5 then challenges White's g-pawn conversion.
defensiveStudy.continuation: White retains g2 and has K g3, while Black has only its king after the h-pawn is removed. Conversion still requires accurate king play.
defensiveStudy.misconception: A king escape from h1 is not always passive: after ...h2+ White can capture the last black pawn. But a reckless g-pawn push can give the distant king counterplay.
defensiveStudy.reflection: Rebuild the white king on g3 and white pawn on g2 after the last move; identify Black's most useful king approach and why the h-pawn has vanished. Compare both routes to Kxh2.

variations.label: Escape first, capture second
variations.explanation: Kh1 delays the capture on h2 until the fifth ply. Black's king steps to f5, and White still removes the h2 passer; however, king activity differs.

variations.label: Tempting immediate pawn race
variations.explanation: g4 is attacked by the black king on f5 and can be captured later. Pushing the remaining pawn before securing its route can squander the conversion.

conversionStudy.context: Only one pawn per side, reflected to g/h files; local liquidation must be assessed with king support.

positions.title: The last dangerous pawn and the active king — Ph2
positions.sourceLabel: P102 · Defending the worse pawn ending
positions.prompt: The defender's black a3 pawn can give a checking threat on a2, but White's king may capture the pawn if it chooses its square accurately. White has a second h-pawn; a local b-versus-a exchange would not leave bare kings. Work both king routes and identify when an apparent pawn win gives the defender a tempo.
positions.replyReason: ...a2 attacks the white king on b1; Kxa2 captures it without entering the black king's attack from b4. In this variation, White has a second h-pawn; a local b-versus-a exchange would not leave bare kings.
positions.continuationReason: At the fifth ply White retains its b-pawn after the capture. The king positions must still be evaluated for conversion or a draw.
positions.explanation: The last dangerous pawn and the active king. Five-ply line a1b1 a3a2 b1a2 b4c5 a2b3. Resistance a1b1 a3a2 b1a1 b4c5 a1a2. Plausible different choice a1b1 b4c5 b2b4. The defender's black a3 pawn can give a checking threat on a2, but White's king may capture the pawn if it chooses its square accurately. ...a2 attacks the white king on b1; Kxa2 captures it without entering the black king's attack from b4. Endpoint: White retains its b-pawn after the capture. The king positions must still be evaluated for conversion or a draw. Misconception: Immediately exchanging the last two pawns by bxa3 Kxa3 would be a draw in the pure case; avoid giving the opposing king a free recapture. Pawn reserve: White has a second h-pawn; a local b-versus-a exchange would not leave bare kings. A concrete two-king draw after liquidation is exact only in the pure case; other WDL values require independent proof.
